---
title: "Showing a Message from the Web"
unit: 3
cluster: "Connecting to the Internet"
---

A board on Wi-Fi can fetch a page from a web server, the same way a Python
program on a computer does. MicroPython has the `urequests` module for this:
a small version of `requests`, with the same `get()`, `status_code` and
`text`.

In this chapter, we'll learn how to:

- put a message on the web, in our `public_html` on the course server
- fetch it from the board with `urequests.get()`
- add a `read_url()` function to the `wifi` module
- show it on the display, and change it from anywhere

## Putting a message on the web

Whatever is in `public_html` on the course server is on the web. We keep the
board's files together, in a directory of their own there. Log in to the
server:

```session
$ ssh coc.apucomputing.in
```

Make the directory, and go into it:

```session
anand@coc:~$ mkdir -p public_html/esp32
anand@coc:~$ cd public_html/esp32
```

`-p` tells `mkdir` not to complain if the directory is already there, so the
command is safe to run again.

Write a message into a file:

```session
anand@coc:~/public_html/esp32$ echo Hello from the web > message.txt
```

Open <https://coc.apucomputing.in/~anand/esp32/message.txt> in the browser,
with your own username in place of `anand`. It shows `Hello from the web`. Stay
logged in to the server: we change the message later.

## Fetching it from the board

Connect Thonny to the board, and connect to the Wi-Fi with the `wifi`
module we saved on the board:

```session
>>> import wifi
```

```session
>>> wifi.connect("MyPhone", "mypassword")
'192.168.43.57'
```

Now fetch the message, with your own username in the URL:

```session
>>> import urequests
```

```session
>>> response = urequests.get("https://coc.apucomputing.in/~anand/esp32/message.txt")
```

The response has the status code and the text, as it does on the computer:

```session
>>> response.status_code
200
```

```session
>>> response.text
'Hello from the web\n'
```

The text ends with `\n`, the newline that `echo` wrote at the end of the
file. `strip()` takes it off:

```session
>>> response.text.strip()
'Hello from the web'
```

A response keeps its connection to the server open until it is closed. The
board can keep only a few connections open at a time, so close each
response once we have read it:

```session
>>> response.close()
```

A URL with no file behind it gives the status code 404, and the text of the
server's error page instead of a message:

```session
>>> response = urequests.get("https://coc.apucomputing.in/~anand/esp32/no-file.txt")
```

```session
>>> response.status_code
404
```

```session
>>> response.close()
```

## A function for reading a URL

A program that reads a URL has to check the status code, and close the
response. We put these steps in a function, `read_url()`, in the `wifi`
module.

Open `wifi.py` from the board: choose **File → Open**, click
**MicroPython device**, and choose `wifi.py`. Add `import urequests` at the
top, and the `read_url()` function at the end. The whole file is now:

```python
import network
import urequests
import time


def list_networks():
    wlan = network.WLAN(network.STA_IF)
    wlan.active(True)
    for found in wlan.scan():
        name = found[0].decode()
        strength = found[3]
        print(name, strength)


def connect(ssid, password):
    wlan = network.WLAN(network.STA_IF)
    wlan.active(True)
    if not wlan.isconnected():
        wlan.connect(ssid, password)
        seconds = 0
        while not wlan.isconnected() and seconds < 15:
            time.sleep(1)
            seconds += 1
    if not wlan.isconnected():
        return None
    return wlan.ifconfig()[0]


def read_url(url):
    response = urequests.get(url)
    status = response.status_code
    text = response.text
    response.close()
    if status != 200:
        print("Could not read", url, "- status code", status)
        return ""
    return text
```

Save the file with **File → Save**.

`read_url()` fetches the URL, and keeps the status code and the text before
it closes the response. It returns the text of the page, or prints the status
code and returns an empty string, `""`. Either way, it returns a string, so
the program that called it can use it the same way.

The REPL still has the old `wifi` module imported. Click **Stop** to restart
MicroPython on the board, and import the module again:

```session
>>> import wifi
```

```session
>>> wifi.connect("MyPhone", "mypassword")
'192.168.43.57'
```

```session
>>> wifi.read_url("https://coc.apucomputing.in/~anand/esp32/message.txt")
'Hello from the web\n'
```

```session
>>> wifi.read_url("https://coc.apucomputing.in/~anand/esp32/no-file.txt")
Could not read https://coc.apucomputing.in/~anand/esp32/no-file.txt - status code 404
''
```

## Showing it on the display

We use the circuit with the display. Plug in the USB cable, and type this
program in the editor, with your own hotspot and username:

```python
from machine import I2C, Pin
from machine_i2c_lcd import I2cLcd
import time
import wifi

i2c = I2C(0, sda=Pin(4), scl=Pin(5), freq=100000)
lcd = I2cLcd(i2c, 39, 2, 16)

url = "https://coc.apucomputing.in/~anand/esp32/message.txt"

lcd.clear()
lcd.putstr("Connecting...")
ip = wifi.connect("MyPhone", "mypassword")
lcd.clear()

if ip is None:
    lcd.putstr("No Wi-Fi")
else:
    while True:
        message = wifi.read_url(url).strip()
        lcd.clear()
        lcd.putstr(message)
        time.sleep(10)
```

The program shows `Connecting...` while it joins the Wi-Fi, which takes a
few seconds. If it cannot join, it shows `No Wi-Fi`, and stops.

Once it is connected, the loop fetches the message every 10 seconds, clears
the display, and writes the message on it.

When the file is missing, `read_url()` returns `""`, so the display is
blank. The Shell shows the status code, and the loop tries again 10 seconds
later.

Click Run. After a few seconds, the display shows `Hello from the web`.

Now change the message on the server:

```session
anand@coc:~/public_html/esp32$ echo Class at 2 pm > message.txt
```

Within 10 seconds, the display shows `Class at 2 pm`. Anyone who can log in
to the server, from anywhere, can now change what the board shows.

## Longer messages

The display shows two lines of 16 characters. A message longer than 16
characters goes on to the second line. A newline in the file also starts the
second line, so a file with two lines shows on the two lines of the display.
Edit the file with `nano` on the server, and write:

```text
Class at 2 pm
Room 204
```

Within 10 seconds, the display shows `Class at 2 pm` on the first line and
`Room 204` on the second. After the second line, the text goes back to the
first, and writes over it, so keep a message to 32 characters.

::: {.callout-warning}
If the board loses the Wi-Fi while the program runs, `urequests.get()` fails
with an `OSError`, and the program stops. The display keeps the last
message, so it looks as if the program is still running. Check the Shell,
and run the program again.
:::

## Summary

A board connected to Wi-Fi fetches a page with `urequests.get()`, and a
program that fetches it in a loop shows the latest version, so the page
changes what the board does.

| Code or command | What it does |
|-----------------|--------------|
| `mkdir -p public_html/esp32`, on the server | makes the directory, with no error if it is already there |
| `echo text > message.txt`, in `public_html/esp32` | puts the text on the web, at `https://coc.apucomputing.in/~username/esp32/message.txt` |
| `import urequests` | the module for fetching URLs; built into MicroPython on the board |
| `response = urequests.get(url)` | fetches the URL; the board must be connected to Wi-Fi first |
| `response.status_code` | `200` if the page was found, `404` if there is nothing at that URL |
| `response.text.strip()` | the text of the page, without the newline at its end |
| `response.close()` | closes the connection to the server; the board can keep only a few open |
| `wifi.read_url(url)` | from `wifi.py` on the board: returns the text of the page, or prints the status code and returns `""` |
| `lcd.putstr(message)` | writes the message; past 16 characters, or at a newline, it goes on to the second line |
| `OSError` from `urequests.get()` | the board could not reach the server, often because it lost the Wi-Fi; the program stops |
